land.text: the Sui empire, taken piecemeal from Emperor Yang's successors and the warlords between the occupation of Chang'an in winter 617 and the defeat of Liang Shidu in 628

predecessors.note: Cliopatria keeps a Sui row to 627; those are the Sui remnants and rival regimes, not the Sui court, which ended in 618-619.

land.text: Gao Kaidao's territory at Youzhou (Cliopatria row 623-625)

predecessors.note: A Cliopatria row only; none of the pages opened mentions Gao Kaidao. A gap-filler should open 'Transition from Sui to Tang'.

land.text: most of northern China (the Later Liang page); Shaanxi (Qi), Hebei (Yan) and Shanxi (Jin) remained largely outside Later Liang control

successors.note: Cliopatria starts the Later Liang in 911; the dynasty was established 1 June 907.

land.text: Shanxi, Li Keyong's and Li Cunxu's State of Jin

successors.note: Cliopatria has two Jin rows (Later Jin 911-946 and Former Jin 922-925); the East Asia research agent should settle which is Li Keyong's Jin from 907.

land.text: Shaanxi west of the capital, Li Maozhen's Qi

capitals.name: Luoyang, as Shendu
capitals.note: Wu Zetian's capital, renamed Shendu (Divine Capital).

capitals.name: Luoyang
capitals.note: Zhu Wen forced the court to Luoyang in 903-904; infobox: Luoyang 904-907.

rulers.name: Wu Zetian, Emperor of Zhou
rulers.title: Empress regnant (Wu Zhou interregnum)
rulers.note: Proclaimed 17 October 690; deposed 21 February 705. Same state, same colour (rule 2).

rulers.name: Xuanzong (Li Longji)
rulers.note: Abdicated 12 August 756 during the An Lushan rebellion.

rulers.name: Ai (Li Zhu)
rulers.note: The emperor list gives his deposition as 12 May 907; the Tang page dates the abdication in favour of Later Liang to 1 June 907.

correction.text: Guanzhong (Chang'an, occupied in winter 617) and the Fen valley around Taiyuan, where Li Yuan had been governor: the Tang at its proclamation on 18 June 618

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's first Tang shape begins in 623 but the dynasty was proclaimed in 618. The ledger's 621 (Hulao) and 628 (Liang Shidu) events carry the growth from this core to the 623 shape.

1.43 M km2 for 623-625: north China after Hulao (621). The pages opened do not date the conquest of the south (Xiao Xian's Liang, Fu Gongshi), so the shape stands; a gap-filler should open 'Transition from Sui to Tang'. Cliopatria's Sui row to 627 and Gao Kaidao 623-625 are the rival remnants.
3.23 M km2: the south (Lingnan, Jiaozhi) now inside; 'Civil war in China was almost totally diminished by 626'.
628-629: the Ordos after Liang Shidu's defeat in 628.

630-632, 3.55 M km2, bbox to 42.6 N: the Eastern Turkic lands south of the Gobi after Illig Qaghan's capture in 630; the Ashina settled in the Ordos Loop as a vassal khaganate, which rule 4 draws as a tint.

correction.text: the shape without the Mongolian Plateau north of the Gobi: Zhenzhu Khan of the Xueyantuo (629-645) 'ruled much of the north'; the plateau came under the Yanran protectorate only in 647

keyframe_review.note: 6.06 M km2 with a bbox to 52.9 N (Lake Baikal) is 14 years early for the steppe.

correction.text: the shape without the Mongolian Plateau (Xueyantuo until 645; Yanran protectorate from 647)

keyframe_review.note: 638-640: the Ashina buffer state between the Yellow River and the Gobi (639-645) is Tang vassal land; the plateau beyond is not Tang.

correction.text: the shape without the Mongolian Plateau until 646; Gaochang (640) and Karasahr (644) in the Tarim are right

keyframe_review.note: 641-646, bbox west to 81.7 E: the Turpan basin and Karasahr after the 640 and 644 conquests.

correction.text: the shape as drawn, but the Mongolian Plateau (the Yanran protectorate's six commanderies and seven tributary prefectures under the jimi system, 647-682) as vassal tint, not direct rule

keyframe_review.note: 647-655, 6.56 M km2: Kucha (648) and the Four Garrisons in the west; the steppe under indirect rule.

correction.text: the shape as drawn (Dzungaria and the Chu-Ili valleys after the Western Turkic Khaganate was annexed in 657), with the Mongolian Plateau as vassal tint

keyframe_review.note: 656-660, 7.33 M km2, bbox west to 73.2 E: 'By the end of the 657 campaign, the Tang had reached its largest extent.'

correction.text: direct rule as in the 656-660 shape; everything west of the Pamirs (Sogdia, Tokharistan, to 58 E in this shape) as vassal tint: the pages opened describe Tang 'influence in Transoxiana', not rule

keyframe_review.note: 661-665 is Cliopatria's largest Tang shape, 8.73 M km2, reaching Khorasan; the Tang page's only area figure is 5.4 M km2 for 715. The Western Turks page describes Tang control as the Tarim oasis states with Turfan as a base and never mentions Sogdia or Tokharistan.

correction.text: without the Tuyuhun lands around Qinghai Lake (Tibetan from 663) and without Transoxiana and Tokharistan (vassal tint at most); from 670 also without the Four Garrisons of the Tarim (Tibetan 670-679)

keyframe_review.note: 666-673, 7.65 M km2, bbox west to 71.3 E. Cliopatria ends its Tuyuhun row in 665 but keeps the land in the Tang shape.

correction.text: without Korea south of the Taedong River, which 'Silla recaptured' in 676 while 'Tang held control over former Goguryeo territory north of Taedong River'; the Tarim is Tang again 679-686

keyframe_review.note: 674-681, 6.30 M km2, bbox east to 131.75 E: the whole former Goguryeo and Baekje. Cliopatria's Unified Silla row begins only in 682.

682-691, 3.55 M km2, bbox north only to 43.3 N: after the Second Turkic Khaganate (682) took the steppe and the Tang withdrew from the Four Garrisons (686); Korea north of the Taedong still Tang (Andong at Xincheng from 677).
692-704, 4.25 M km2, bbox west to 73.1 E: the Four Garrisons recovered by Wang Xiaojie in 692. The Wu Zhou years (690-705) are the same state (rule 2).
705-749, 4.03 M km2 for 45 years; the infobox gives 5.4 M km2 for 715 (ratio 0.75, within the factor-of-two check). The Beiting protectorate north of the Tianshan is inside the shape.

correction.text: without the plateau north of the Gobi: the Anbei protectorate's seat had retreated to Hengsai near Urad Middle Banner by 749, and the Uyghur Khaganate holds the steppe (Cliopatria's own Uyghur row begins in 750)

keyframe_review.note: 750, 4.59 M km2, bbox north to 47.1 N, which is 5 degrees north of the Tang's last protectorate seats.

correction.text: without the plateau north of the Gobi (Uyghur); the west is right: after Talas (July 751) 'no significant loss or gain of territory occurred and the borders remained relatively unchanged'

keyframe_review.note: 751-754, 4.65 M km2, bbox west to 72.1 E.

correction.text: without the steppe (Uyghur) and without the land the Yan rebels hold: Hebei from An Lushan's march out of Fanyang on 16 December 755, Luoyang from 18 January 756, and Chang'an with Guanzhong from July 756

keyframe_review.note: 755-756, 4.52 M km2: Cliopatria has no Yan (An Lushan) polity, so the rebel-held land needs a dossier of type rebel (see notes) and rule 5's hatched fill.

correction.text: Hexi stays Tang until Tibet conquers Liang Prefecture in 764; the Anxi and Beiting protectorates, cut off from 764, hold out until 787 (Kucha), c. 790 (the protectorate's end) and 792 (Khotan); Luoyang is rebel-held 759-762

keyframe_review.note: 757-762, 3.09 M km2, bbox west only to 100.9 E: Cliopatria removes Hexi and the Western Regions in 757, seven years before Liangzhou fell and thirty before Kucha. The ledger dates the losses.

correction.text: the isolated Anxi and Beiting garrisons remain Tang (soft edge) until 787-792; Hexi is Tibetan from 764 (Liangzhou first, the rest of the corridor over the following decades)

keyframe_review.note: 763-767, 3.06 M km2. Chang'an was Tibetan-occupied for fifteen days from 18 November 763 (hatched, rule 4).

correction.text: as drawn from 792; before that add the Anxi and Beiting garrisons in the Tarim, Dzungaria and the Turpan basin, whose losses (787 Kucha, c. 790 Beiting, 792 Khotan) the ledger dates

keyframe_review.note: 768-829, 3.09 M km2 for 62 years; the 783 treaty 'defined the borders' with Tibet, so the Tibetan frontier is sharp from 783 (certainty).
830-849, 2.89 M km2: Nanzhao's raid on Chengdu in 829 took nothing ('withdrew the following year').

correction.text: with Zhang Yichao's prefectures (Shazhou and Guazhou 848; Ganzhou, Suzhou and Yizhou by 850; Xizhou 851) as Tang vassal land, the Guiyi Circuit, 'usually de facto independent but nominally subordinate'

keyframe_review.note: 850-859, 2.91 M km2. Cliopatria gives Hexi to 'Tibetans' (850-) and 'Ganzhou Kingdom' (860-) instead of the Guiyi Circuit; the Tang page says the Tang 'managed to restore indirect control over former territories as far west as the Hexi Corridor'.

correction.text: with Guiyi's Hexi (Liangzhou too from 861) as vassal land, and without Annan, which Nanzhao occupied from 863 'for three years' until Gao Pian retook it in fall 866
with the Guiyi Circuit's Hexi as vassal land; Annan is Tang again from fall 866

keyframe_review.note: 866-874, 3.12 M km2. Nanzhao's 869 siege of Chengdu and 873-874 raid held no ground.

correction.text: with the Guiyi Circuit's Hexi as vassal land (Yizhou was lost to Qocho in 876)

keyframe_review.note: 875-877: Huang Chao's rebellion (874-884) is a roving army in these years and holds no fixed territory.

correction.text: with the Guiyi Circuit's Hexi as vassal land

keyframe_review.note: 878-879: the Huang Chao page does not date the capture of Guangzhou, so nothing is removed.

correction.text: with Guiyi's Hexi as vassal land and without Guanzhong from 16 January 881, when Huang Chao 'moved into the Tang palace in Chang'an and declared himself the emperor of a new state of Qi'

keyframe_review.note: 880-881. Cliopatria has no Qi (Huang Chao) polity: a rebel dossier is needed (see notes).

correction.text: with Guiyi's Hexi as vassal land and without Guanzhong until summer 883, when 'Li Keyong entered Chang'an, and Huang was unable to resist him, and so abandoned Chang'an to flee east'
with the Guiyi Circuit's Hexi as vassal land; the jiedushi are autonomous but the sources still call their circuits Tang

keyframe_review.note: 884-899, 3.12 M km2. Huang Chao killed 13 July 884.

correction.text: with the Guiyi Circuit's Hexi as vassal land, and ending in June 907, not 910: 'In 907, the Tang dynasty was ended when Zhu deposed Ai and took the throne for himself'

keyframe_review.note: 900-910: Cliopatria keeps the Tang to 910 and starts the Later Liang and the Ten Kingdoms in 911; the four years 907-910 belong to the successors (identity.successors).

region.text: Chang'an, occupied in winter 617, and Taiyuan, where Li Yuan had been governor

ledger.note: 618: Li Yuan proclaims the Tang at Chang'an. 'Li Yuan declared himself emperor of the newly founded Tang dynasty' on 18 June 618, after news of Emperor Yang's murder; infobox 'Established: June 18, 618'. The page gives the cities, not a boundary.

region.text: Luoyang and Dou Jiande's Hebei, after the Battle of Hulao

ledger.note: 621: Li Shimin wins at Hulao. 'he defeated Dou Jiande (573–621) at Luoyang in the Battle of Hulao on May 28, 621.' Wang Shichong's Zheng at Luoyang is not on the page.

region.text: the Ordos, Liang Shidu's territory

ledger.note: 628: the last warlord falls. 'Civil war in China was almost totally diminished by 626, along with the 628 defeat of the Ordos warlord Liang Shidu.'

region.text: areas of the Ordos Desert and the Eastern Turkic lands south of the Gobi

ledger.note: 630: the Eastern Turks fall. 'In 630, Tang armies captured areas of the Ordos Desert'; 'The Tang dynasty overthrew the Eastern Turkic Khaganate in 630' and Illig was captured (Eastern Turkic Khaganate page).

region.text: the Ashina settled inside the Ordos Loop, then between the Yellow River and the Gobi

ledger.note: 630-645: the Turks as Tang vassals. Infobox 'Vassal khaganate of the Tang dynasty (630–639)' and 'Buffer state of the Tang dynasty (639–645)'; 'Taizong made the Ashina live inside the Ordos Loop'; driven south of the river by the Xueyantuo in 642; 'Reconquest by Tang dynasty: 645'.

region.text: the Tuyuhun around Qinghai Lake

ledger.note: 634: the Tuyuhun become a Tang vassal (infobox 'Vassal of the Tang dynasty: 634'). The Tang page records 'separate campaigns against the Tuyuhun' under Taizong without a date.

region.text: Gaochang (Turpan), made Xi Prefecture, seat of the Anxi Protectorate from 11 October 640

ledger.note: 640: Gaochang conquered; the Anxi protectorate founded. Hou Junji conquers Gaochang on 19 September 640; 'Xi Prefecture became the seat of the Anxi Protectorate on 11 October.' Cliopatria has no Gaochang polity; the oasis is drawn as Western Göktürk land before 640.

region.text: Karasahr (Yanqi), conquered in 644; Aksu garrisoned

ledger.note: 644: Karasahr taken. The Western Turks page dates a first annexation to 644 and a second campaign under Ashina She'er in 648 after a usurper backed by Kucha and the Western Turks.

region.text: the Ashina buffer state between the Yellow River and the Gobi

ledger.note: 645: the buffer khaganate ends with the Tang reconquest (infobox 'Reconquest by Tang dynasty: 645'); Chebi Khan's revival attempt (646-650) fails. Cliopatria ends its Eastern Göktürks row in 632.

region.text: from Lake Baikal to the north, the Gobi Desert to the south, the Greater Khingan to the east and the Altai Mountains to the west: the former Xueyantuo territory

ledger.note: 647: the steppe submits; the Yanran protectorate founded. Thirteen Tiele and Uyghur tribes surrender on 9 January 647 and are organised into 'six commanderies and seven tributary prefectures under the Jimi system'; the Yanran Protectorate, created 10 April 647, 'controlled the Mongolian Plateau from 647 to 682'. Indirect rule: vassal tint (rule 4), not the direct colour Cliopatria draws from 633.

region.text: Kucha, the new seat of Anxi, and the Four Garrisons: Kucha, Khotan, Kashgar, Karasahr

ledger.note: 648: Kucha falls; the Four Garrisons. Kucha surrendered on 19 January 649 per the Western Turks page; 'The Four Garrisons (Kucha, Khotan, Kashgar, Karasahr) were installed between 648 and 658.' Khotan and Kashgar had submitted as tributaries in 632.

region.text: the Western Turkic Khaganate's lands north of the Tianshan and in the Chu and Ili valleys (Suyab), after Su Dingfang's victory on the Irtysh

ledger.note: 657: the Western Turks fall; the Tang at its largest. Su Dingfang 'defeated Helu's army of 100,000 cavalry' at the Irtysh River in 657 and the khaganate was annexed: 'By the end of the 657 campaign, the Tang had reached its largest extent.' The page describes Tang control as the Tarim oasis states with Turfan as a base; it does not mention Sogdia or Tokharistan.

region.text: the kingdom of Baekje, 'toppled in 660 by a Tang–Silla invasion'

ledger.note: 660: Baekje destroyed. Tang commanderies on former Baekje land until Silla expels the Tang in 671-676.

region.text: Sogdia and Tokharistan, where the Tang had 'influence in Transoxiana' rather than rule

ledger.note: 661: the lands west of the Pamirs as Tang clients. The year is Cliopatria's (its 661-665 shape reaches 58 E), not a page's; the Talas page says the 751 defeat 'marked the end of Tang influence in Transoxiana', so influence existed. A gap-filler should open 'Protectorate General to Pacify the West' sections on the sixteen jimi protectorates of 661, or the Wikipedia article on Tokharistan.

region.text: the Azha or Tuyuhun kingdom, 'defeated by the Tibetan army and gradually assimilated into Tibetan culture'

ledger.note: 663: the Tuyuhun fall to Tibet (tibetan-empire takes the land). The Tuyuhun page's infobox gives 'Destroyed by the Tibetan Empire: 670' instead and Cliopatria ends the row in 665; the Tibetan Empire page's 663 is used, the ruling house having fled east under Murong Nuohebo.

region.text: Goguryeo's territory in Manchuria and the northern Korean Peninsula, 'divided into 9 commanderies, 42 prefectures, and 100 counties' under the Protectorate General to Pacify the East at Pyongyang

ledger.note: 668: Goguryeo destroyed; the Andong protectorate at Pyongyang. 'the Kingdom of Goguryeo was destroyed by 668' (Tang page); the protectorate 'created in Pyongyang'. Goguryeo revolted in 669.

region.text: all of the Chinese Four Garrisons of Anxi in the Tarim Basin; the seat withdrawn to Suyab

ledger.note: 670: the Four Garrisons fall to Tibet. 'In 670 the Tibetan Empire routed a Tang army at the Battle of Dafei River', captured Qiuci (Kucha) and the seat moved to Suyab; Tibet 'gained control over all of the Chinese Four Garrisons of Anxi in the Tarim Basin in 670' (Tibetan Empire page). Cliopatria keeps the Tarim in the Tang shape until 681.

region.text: former Baekje and the Goguryeo lands south of the Taedong River

ledger.note: 670: the Silla–Tang War begins. 'From 670 to 675, Goguryeo loyalists aligned with Silla launched offensives against the Tang Chinese on all fronts' (Andong page); 'Silla broke the alliance in 671' (Tang page).

region.text: the territory south of the Taedong River

ledger.note: 676: the war ends in Silla's favour. 'Silla took all the territory south of the Taedong River in a series of battles in 676'; the Andong seat moves to Liaoyang (second month of 676), then Xincheng (677).

region.text: 'Silla recaptured the territory south of Taedong River'; 'Tang held control over former Goguryeo territory north of Taedong River'

ledger.note: 676: Korea south of the Taedong passes to Silla. Infobox result: 'Silla victory. Silla controls the peninsula south of the Taedong River, and Tang keeps the Liaodong area.' Cliopatria's Silla row ends 681 and Unified Silla begins 682; the loss should be shown in 676.

region.text: the Four Garrisons, control re-established by Pei Xingjian; Tokmak (Suyab) annexed as a military base

ledger.note: 679: the Tarim recovered. 'Pei Xingjian defeats the Tibetans and re-establishes control'; an earlier swing (control returned 673-675, Qiuci lost again in 677) is in the same page.

region.text: the plateau the Yanran/Anbei protectorate 'controlled from 647 to 682'

ledger.note: 682: the steppe is lost to the Second Turkic Khaganate of Ilterish Qaghan ('Second Turkic Khaganate established: 682', Eastern Turkic page). The Chanyu protectorate was besieged in 683 and downgraded in 686. Cliopatria's 'Türgesh' row (692-749, in Mongolia) is probably this khaganate under the wrong name (notes).

region.text: the Four Garrisons, from which Tang troops withdrew in 686; 'Tibet establishes control over the Western Regions' in 687

ledger.note: 687: the Tarim lost again.

690: Wu Zetian proclaims the Zhou. Established 17 October 690 with herself as huangdi, having deposed Ruizong; 'Historians generally regard the Wu Zhou as an interregnum of the Tang dynasty': same state, same colour (rule 2), an era caption as the reference video does.
690: the capital is Luoyang, renamed Shendu (Divine Capital).

region.text: the Western Regions, pacified by Wang Xiaojie; the Anxi Protectorate re-established at Qiuci

ledger.note: 692: Wang Xiaojie recovers the Four Garrisons. 'Tang troops under Wang Xiaojie pacified the Western Regions and established the Anxi Protectorate at Qiuci'; 'In 692, the Tibetans lost the Tarim Basin to the Chinese' (Tibetan Empire page).

705: the Tang restored. The Shenlong coup restores Zhongzong; Wu Zetian abdicated the next day (21-22 February 705) and 'the so-called Zhou dynasty fizzled to an end with the restoration of the Tang'; 'the Tang was formally restored on March 3' (Tang page).
705: the court returns to Chang'an (infobox: Chang'an 618-690 and 705-904).

region.text: Nanzhao, Piluoge's united Six Zhao around Dali

ledger.note: 738: Nanzhao recognised as a Tang tributary. 'In the year 737 AD, Piluoge united the Six Zhaos in succession'; the Tang granted him 'the Chinese-style name Meng Guiyi' and a title; infobox established 738. Cliopatria's Nanzhao row begins 741.

region.text: Nanzhao, after the Tang defeat at Xiaguan

ledger.note: 751: Nanzhao breaks with the Tang. Xianyu Zhongtong's army 'was defeated by Duan Jianwei with heavy losses (many due to disease) at Xiaguan'; 'By the end of 754, Geluofeng had established an alliance with the Tibetans against the Tang that would last until 794'; the Tibetan Empire page says Nanzhao 'remained under Tibetan control from 750 to 794'.

region.text: Transoxania: 'End of Tang presence in Transoxania'

ledger.note: July 751: the Battle of Talas; the abbasid-caliphate takes the Tang's place in Transoxiana. Gao Xianzhi's army 'was defeated by the Abbasid army under Ziyad ibn Salih and Karluk mercenaries'; 'The defeat marked the end of Tang influence in Transoxiana and halted Tang westward expansion', but 'no significant loss or gain of territory occurred and the borders remained relatively unchanged', so only the influence west of the Pamirs ends; the Tarim garrisons stay.

region.text: Fanyang (Youzhou) and Hebei, An Lushan's base

ledger.note: 755: An Lushan rebels. On 16 December 755 he 'mobilized his army and marched out of Fanyang'; he 'declared himself Emperor of the new Great Yan dynasty' on 5 February 756. The rebel state needs a dossier of type rebel (notes).

region.text: the Yellow River plain between Fanyang, Luoyang and Tongguan, where the fighting ran until 763

ledger.note: 755-763: the An Lushan rebellion's fighting zone (rule 6 blend where neither side holds firmly). Yongqiu (spring 756) 'prevented the Yan forces from conquering southern China'.

region.text: the Eastern Capital, Luoyang

ledger.note: 756: Luoyang falls to the rebels. He 'captured the "Eastern Capital" city of Luoyang on 18 January 756'.

region.text: the capital Chang'an and Guanzhong, after the defeat at Tongguan on 7 July 756

ledger.note: 756: Chang'an falls. 'In July 756 An Lushan and his rebel forces captured Chang'an'; Xuanzong flees toward Sichuan and abdicates on 12 August; Suzong 'was proclaimed Emperor Suzong at Lingzhou'; Uyghur help sought in 756.

region.text: both Chang'an and Luoyang

ledger.note: 757: the capitals recovered. 'With Uyghur assistance, the Tang Imperial forces recaptured both Chang'an and Luoyang in late 757'; An Lushan had been killed by his son on 29 January 757; An Qingxu 'abandoned Luoyang and fled north' to Yecheng.

region.text: Bian (Kaifeng) and Luoyang, taken by Shi Siming

ledger.note: 759: Luoyang falls again. Shi Siming kills An Qingxu on 10 April 759, is enthroned as Emperor Zhaowu of Yan and takes Bian and Luoyang (the page gives no exact date for Luoyang); the front stalemates at Heyang and Shan.

region.text: Luoyang, retaken for the second time in winter 762

ledger.note: 762: Luoyang recovered. 'Winter 762: Tang forces retook Luoyang for a second time.'

region.text: the rebellion's fighting zone

ledger.note: 763: the An Lushan rebellion ends. 'Shi Chaoyi killed himself rather than be captured' on 17 February 763; infobox 'Tang victory'.

region.text: Hebei, where surrendered Yan generals keep their posts as jiedushi

ledger.note: 763: Hebei returns to the Tang in name. 'In Hebei, three fanzhen became virtually independent for the remainder of the Tang dynasty': drawn as Tang because the sources call them Tang jiedushi; a vassal tint would be defensible and the reviewer may ask for it.

region.text: Chang'an, occupied for fifteen days from 18 November 763

ledger.note: 763: Tibet in Chang'an. Tibetan forces 'proceeded to briefly capture Chang'an on 18 November 763'; they 'occupied Chang'an for fifteen days and installed a puppet emperor' (Tibetan Empire page). Hatched, rule 4; not a change of owner.

region.text: Chang'an

ledger.note: 763: the Tibetans leave Chang'an after fifteen days.

region.text: Liang Prefecture (Liangzhou), 'cutting off the Anxi and Beiting protectorates from the Tang dynasty'; the rest of the corridor (Ganzhou, Suzhou, Guazhou, Shazhou) over the following decades

ledger.note: 764: Tibet takes Liangzhou and cuts off the west. The pages opened date only Liangzhou; the ledger places the whole corridor's loss here (confidence 2) and the window agent may stage it westward; a gap-filler should open 'Hexi Corridor' or 'Tibetan attack on Chang'an' for the dates of Ganzhou, Suzhou, Guazhou and Shazhou (781-787 in the usual accounts).

region.text: Longyou and Hexi, fought over until the 783 treaty

ledger.note: 764-783: the Tang–Tibetan war for Longyou and Hexi after the An Lushan rebellion; Tibet 'conquer[ed] much of the western half of Tang territories' (An Lushan page).

region.text: the Tang–Tibetan frontier as the 783 treaty 'defined the borders'

ledger.note: 783: the Treaty of Qingshui. 'a 783 treaty between the Tibetan Empire and the Tang dynasty defined the borders' (the page does not name it); Longyou and Hexi stay Tibetan. The frontier is sharp from here (certainty).

region.text: Qiuci (Kucha), seat of the Anxi protectorate

ledger.note: 787: Kucha falls. 'In 787 the Tibetan Empire conquered Qiuci.' The garrison had been cut off since 764 (Guo Xin and Li Yuanzhong made protectors general in 780); the officeholder list keeps Guo Xin to 808, which the page's narrative contradicts.

region.text: the Beiting protectorate north of the Tianshan and the Turpan basin: 'By 790 Chinese control over the Tarim Basin was completely lost'

ledger.note: c. 790: the protectorates end. 'the last vestiges of the protectorate and its garrisons were defeated by Tibetan forces by 790' (Anxi page). The Beiting Protectorate page opened is a stub with no dates, so 790 for Beiting itself is the researcher's reading (confidence 1); the Uyghur Khaganate, not Tibet, may have taken parts of Dzungaria.

region.text: Yutian (Khotan)

ledger.note: 792: Khotan falls, the last garrison. 'In 792 the Tibetan Empire conquered Yutian.'

region.text: Nanzhao, which 'switched sides to the Tang' after the battle of Shenchuan

ledger.note: 794: Nanzhao returns to the Tang. 'In 794, he launched the battle of Shenchuan to break up with Tibet and switched sides to the Tang.' A tributary tint; Nanzhao's raids from 829 show how loose it was.

region.text: Shazhou (Dunhuang) and Guazhou, captured 'from the Tibetans'

ledger.note: 848: Zhang Yichao rises at Dunhuang. 'In 848, Zhang Yichao, a resident of Shazhou, led an uprising and captured Shazhou and Guazhou from the Tibetans.' Cliopatria's Tibetan Empire row ends 849 ('Tibetans' from 850); the Tibetan Empire page dates the collapse to 842.

region.text: Ganzhou, Suzhou, and Yizhou

ledger.note: 850: the corridor recovered. 'By 850 Zhang had captured Ganzhou, Suzhou, and Yizhou.' Suzhou (Jiuquan) is given as a coordinate because the gazetteer has no place entry for it.

region.text: Xizhou (Gaochang)

ledger.note: 851: 'In 851 Zhang captured Xizhou (Gaochang).'

region.text: Zhang's territory, named Guiyi Prefecture by the Tang court, 'usually de facto independent but nominally subordinate'

ledger.note: 851: the Guiyi Circuit. The Tang court names Zhang's territory Guiyi Prefecture and makes him Guiyi jiedushi; the Tang 'managed to restore indirect control over former territories as far west as the Hexi Corridor' (Tang page). Vassal tint over the 848-851 gains, with its own outline and label (rule 4); it outlives the Tang (to 1036).

region.text: Liangzhou, with Lanzhou, Hezhou and Kuozhou

ledger.note: 861: Guiyi's authority extends to Liangzhou 'and several other prefectures, including Lanzhou, Hezhou, and Kuozhou'. Vassal land like the rest of the circuit.

region.text: Annan (Songping and Junzhou), occupied 'for three years'

ledger.note: 863: Nanzhao takes Annam. 'Shilong attacked Annan again in 863, occupying it for three years.'

region.text: Annan, retaken by Gao Pian

ledger.note: 866: Annam recovered. 'Gao completed the retaking of Annan in fall 866.'

region.text: the Tang palace in Chang'an and Guanzhong

ledger.note: 881: Huang Chao takes Chang'an. 'In 881, Huang Chao moved into the Tang palace in Chang'an and declared himself the emperor of a new state of Qi' (reign from 16 January 881); 'forcing Emperor Xizong to flee'. The rebel state needs a dossier of type rebel (notes).

region.text: Chang'an, which Huang Chao 'abandoned' when Li Keyong entered it in summer 883

ledger.note: 883: Chang'an retaken. 'In summer 883, Li Keyong entered Chang'an, and Huang was unable to resist him, and so abandoned Chang'an to flee east'; Huang Chao killed on 13 July 884; the rebellion 'permanently destroyed the power of the Tang dynasty'.
904: the court moved to Luoyang. Zhu Wen, who 'seized control of the Tang capital Chang'an' in 901, forces the move in 903-904 and has Zhaozong killed (22 September 904); infobox: Luoyang 904-907.

region.text: the Tang's remaining territory: 'most of northern China' to the Later Liang, while the regional governors keep Sichuan, the Yangtze, Zhejiang, Fujian, Lingnan, Hunan, Shanxi, western Shaanxi and northern Hebei as the Ten Kingdoms, Jin, Qi and Yan

ledger.note: 907: Zhu Wen ends the Tang. 'In 907, the Tang dynasty was ended when Zhu deposed Ai and took the throne for himself'; the Later Liang page's infobox 'Established: 1 June 907' (the emperor list gives Ai's deposition as 12 May 907). Successors and their land in identity.successors; Cliopatria's four extra years (to 910) go to them.

wars.name: Tang campaign against the Eastern Turks

zones.text: the Ordos and the steppe south of the Gobi

wars.outcome: Tang victory: Illig Qaghan captured in 630 and the khaganate overthrown; the Ashina settled in the Ordos Loop as vassals.
wars.note: 'Six Tang armies attacked on a 1,200 km (750 mi) front' in 629 after famine and revolts weakened Illig.

wars.name: Tang campaigns against the Western Turks
wars.outcome: Tang victory; fall of the Western Turkic Khaganate in 657 and the Tang's largest extent. The page's own span is 640-712 (the last Western Turkic remnants absorbed by the Second Turkic Khaganate in 712).

wars.name: Goguryeo–Tang War and the fall of Baekje
wars.outcome: Baekje destroyed in 660 and Goguryeo by 668 by Tang and Silla; the Protectorate General to Pacify the East set up at Pyongyang.
wars.note: The Tang page gives the end dates; the campaigns' own pages were not opened. Contested-zone shading only for Liaodong and the Taedong valley in the years of fighting the campaign pages date.

wars.name: Silla–Tang War

zones.text: the peninsula south of the Taedong River

wars.outcome: Silla victory: Silla controls the peninsula south of the Taedong River, the Tang keep Liaodong and the Goguryeo land north of it; the Andong seat retreats to Liaoyang (676) and Xincheng (677); the Tang formally recognise Silla's control south of the Taedong in 736.

wars.name: Tang–Tibetan war for the Four Garrisons
wars.outcome: Tibet takes the Tarim in 670 (Dafei River), loses it 679, retakes it 687; Wang Xiaojie recovers it for the Tang in 692 and the Anxi Protectorate is re-established at Kucha.
wars.note: A Western Turkic tribe allied with Tibet invaded the Tarim in 670 (Western Turks page). The swings are in the ledger as loss/gain, so no contest shading is needed beyond the years of campaign.

wars.name: Tang–Nanzhao war

zones.text: Xiaguan (751) and the approaches to Dali

wars.outcome: Tang defeated at Xiaguan in 751; Li Mi's 754 army 'never made it past Mu'ege'; Nanzhao allied with Tibet from 754 to 794.
wars.note: No ground changed hands, so the ledger carries only the vassal_end of 751.

wars.name: Battle of Talas
wars.outcome: Abbasid victory in July 751; 'Consolidation of Abbasid rule in Transoxania; End of Tang presence in Transoxania', but 'no significant loss or gain of territory occurred and the borders remained relatively unchanged'; the Tang recovered Gilgit in 753.
wars.note: Empty zones: no cell changes owner; the ledger ends the Transoxiana vassal tint.

wars.name: An Lushan rebellion

zones.text: Luoyang, Bian, the Heyang and Shan fronts

wars.outcome: Tang victory on 17 February 763 (Shi Chaoyi's suicide), with Uyghur help and Abbasid mercenaries; the Western Regions permanently lost to Tibet, the Hebei garrisons virtually independent, warlordism begins.
wars.note: Rebel-held land is the Yan rebel state's (rule 5), the fighting zone between Luoyang and Tongguan the blend (rule 6). Infobox dates 16 December 755 to 17 February 763.

wars.name: Tang–Tibetan war after the An Lushan rebellion

zones.text: Liangzhou 764, then the corridor to Dunhuang
Chang'an, occupied fifteen days in November 763

wars.outcome: Tibet takes Hexi and Longyou and cuts off the Anxi and Beiting protectorates; a 783 treaty defines the borders; the garrisons fall in 787-792. The Tang-Uyghur alliance of 788-789 'twice defeated the Tibetans'.

wars.name: Nanzhao's campaigns against the Tang

zones.text: Chengdu, attacked 829, besieged 869, approached within 70 km in 873-874: no ground held

wars.outcome: Annam lost in 863 and retaken by Gao Pian in fall 866; the Sichuan campaigns held no ground; Shilong's death in 877 'effectively ended Nanzhao's expansionist campaigns'.
wars.note: The Chengdu zone is listed so the reviewer sees it was considered; only Annam enters the ledger.

wars.name: Huang Chao rebellion
wars.outcome: Chang'an retaken by Li Keyong's Shatuo army in summer 883; Huang Chao killed on 13 July 884; the rebellion 'permanently destroyed the power of the Tang dynasty'.
wars.note: A roving army until 880: Guangzhou's capture (879 in the usual accounts) is undated on the page, so no southern zone is shaded.

certainty.note: The steppe, Tarim and Tibetan frontiers are approximate; the provincial frontiers in the south follow Tang circuits; the Korean frontier is the Taedong River from 676.
The Tibetan frontier is sharp from the 783 treaty that 'defined the borders' and the 821/822 treaty; every other frontier stays soft.

notes:
Worked example written by the Phase A briefs agent on 2026-10-18 from the pages listed; it is a real dossier for the Tang, not a template, and the East Asia (Tang and the Five Dynasties) research group should replace it with polities/tang-dynasty.json after review.

Cliopatria rows to correct (all in keyframe_review): the Tang begins 623 instead of 618 and ends 910 instead of 907, with its successors starting 911; the Sui row runs to 627; the Mongolian Plateau is drawn as direct Tang territory 633-681 (Xueyantuo until 645, then jimi protectorate); the 661-673 shapes reach Khorasan; Hexi and the Western Regions are removed in 757 although Liangzhou fell in 764 and Kucha in 787; the Guiyi Circuit's Hexi (848-907) is given to 'Tibetans' and 'Ganzhou Kingdom'.

States Cliopatria lacks that this dossier's counterparts need: Yan (An Lushan, 756-763; slug suggestion yan-an-lushan, type rebel: Hebei, Luoyang 756-757 and 759-762, Chang'an 756-757); Qi (Huang Chao, 881-884; slug qi-huang-chao, type rebel: Guanzhong); the Xueyantuo (629-646, the steppe); the Kingdom of Gaochang (to 640); the Guiyi Circuit (848-1036, nominally Tang; could be a colony/vassal dossier). The Yanran/Anbei, Anxi, Beiting and Andong protectorates are not states: they are the vassal tint over the regions the ledger names.

Disagreements between pages: Tuyuhun's fall 663 (Tibetan Empire page) or 670 (Tuyuhun infobox); Ai's deposition 12 May 907 (emperor list) or the abdication of 1 June 907 (Tang page, Later Liang infobox); Wu Zetian's proclamation 16 October 690 (Tang page) or 17 October (Wu Zhou page); Nanzhao's break with the Tang 750 (Tibetan Empire page), 751 (Xiaguan) or 754 (alliance with Tibet).

Cliopatria labels to check (Inner Asia group): 'Türgesh' 692-749 lies in Mongolia and 'Turks' 666-756 in Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, which looks like swapped names (the Second Turkic Khaganate held Mongolia 682-744, the Türgesh the Chu valley).

Pages that would help a gap-filler: 'Transition from Sui to Tang' (the conquests of 618-628), 'Tang campaign against Tuyuhun', 'Hexi Corridor' or 'Tibetan attack on Chang'an' (the fall of Ganzhou, Suzhou, Guazhou and Shazhou 781-787), 'Beiting Protectorate' is a stub. The Tang page's area is given only for 715 (5.4 M km2); Cliopatria's 705-749 shape is 4.03 M km2 (ratio 0.75) and its 661-665 shape 8.73 M km2.
